examples.en: On weekends the market is bustling with people.

examples.ko: 좁은 방에서 여섯 식구가 복닥거리며 살았어요.
examples.en: Six family members lived crammed together in a small room.
Every morning the subway station is crowded with commuters.
I woke up to the sound of the kids bustling about.
It was a holiday, so the whole family was bustling around in the kitchen.
The airport will be very crowded over the holidays.

explain: 사람이 많이 모여 어수선하게 움직이는 모습이에요. 일상에서는 '북적거리다'도 자주 쓰고, '복닥거리다'는 좁은 곳에 모여 있는 느낌이 있어요. 주로 장소나 사람이 주어예요.
explain_en: It describes many people gathering and moving around in a busy, cluttered way. In daily talk '북적거리다' is also common, and '복닥거리다' suggests a cramped space. The subject is usually a place or people.

en: the dog days of summer; sweltering midsummer heat

examples.en: This year's midsummer heat is really hard to bear.
Many people eat samgyetang during the dog days of summer.
The dog days have passed and the cool autumn has arrived.

examples.ko: 복더위 때문에 밤에도 잠을 잘 못 자요.
examples.en: Because of the midsummer heat, I can't sleep well even at night.

examples.ko: 이 복더위에 밖에서 일하시는 분들이 걱정돼요.
examples.en: I worry about the people working outside in this scorching heat.

examples.ko: 복더위가 끝나면 가족과 바다에 가고 싶어요.
examples.en: When the worst of the summer heat is over, I want to go to the sea with my family.

explain: 초복부터 말복까지, 삼복 동안의 가장 심한 더위예요. '삼복더위'라고도 해요. '폭염'은 기온이 높은 날씨 자체를 말하지만, '복더위'는 삼복이라는 시기의 더위를 가리켜요.
explain_en: It means the fiercest heat of the three bok days, from chobok to malbok. It is also called '삼복더위'. '폭염' describes extremely hot weather itself, while '복더위' refers to the heat of that particular period.

examples.en: Our youngest is the family's bundle of good luck.

examples.ko: 아기가 태어난 뒤로 일이 잘 풀려서 복덩어리라고 불러요.
examples.en: Things went well after the baby was born, so we call him our lucky charm.

examples.ko: 이 강아지는 우리 집에 온 복덩어리가 틀림없어요.
examples.en: This puppy must be a blessing that came to our home.
The new employee seems like a real stroke of luck.
I'm happy that such a blessing of a daughter-in-law joined the family.
I came home from the hospital holding our little bundle of luck.

explain: 집이나 모임에 들어와 좋은 일을 가져다주는 사람에게 애정을 담아 쓰는 말이에요. 아기, 새 식구, 새 직원에게 자주 써요. 비슷한 말로 '복덩이'도 있어요.
explain_en: It is an affectionate word for someone who brings good fortune to a home or group. It is often used for babies, new family members and new coworkers. '복덩이' is a similar word.

examples.en: Hearing my mom's voice makes my sorrow well up.
Grief welled up so much that I couldn't go on speaking.
Joy surged up inside me at the news that I passed.
I couldn't hold back the tears welling up.
My anger surged up and I shouted.

examples.ko: 분노가 복받칠 때는 잠깐 밖에 나가요.
examples.en: When anger wells up, I step outside for a moment.

explain: 설움, 눈물, 분노, 기쁨 같은 감정이 속에서 세게 치밀어 오를 때 써요. '감정이 복받치다' 형태로 쓰고, 감정이 아닌 물건에는 쓰지 않아요. 활용은 '복받쳐요', '복받친' 이에요.
explain_en: Use it when strong feelings such as sorrow, tears, anger or joy rise up from inside. It is used in the pattern 'emotion + 복받치다' and not for physical objects. The forms are '복받쳐요' and '복받친'.

examples.en: An unexpected dark horse showed up in the final.
The hidden danger in this exam is the English listening part.

examples.ko: 생각지도 못한 복병을 만나서 계획이 늦어졌어요.
examples.en: We ran into an unforeseen obstacle and the plan was delayed.

examples.ko: 이 팀은 이번 대회의 복병으로 꼽혀요.
examples.en: This team is regarded as the dark horse of this tournament.
The event was canceled because of the unexpected factor of the weather.

examples.ko: 복병처럼 숨어 있던 문제가 갑자기 드러났어요.
examples.en: A problem that had been lurking like a hidden trap suddenly came to light.

explain: 원래는 숨어서 기다리는 군사를 뜻하지만, 지금은 예상하지 못한 경쟁자나 장애물을 말할 때 많이 써요. 스포츠와 시험, 일 이야기에서 자주 나와요. '복병이 나타나다/숨어 있다'처럼 써요.
explain_en: It originally meant soldiers waiting in hiding, but now it mostly refers to an unexpected rival or obstacle. It often appears in talk about sports, exams and work. It is used as '복병이 나타나다' or '복병이 숨어 있다'.

examples.en: Do you have a plan in mind for solving this problem?

examples.ko: 김 팀장님은 이미 나름의 복안을 갖고 계세요.
examples.en: Team Leader Kim already has a plan of his own in mind.
I can't tell you my plan yet.

examples.ko: 정부는 새 정책에 대한 복안을 발표했어요.
examples.en: The government announced its plan for the new policy.

examples.ko: 아무 복안 없이 시작하면 나중에 힘들어요.
examples.en: If you start without any plan in mind, it gets hard later.

examples.ko: 그 일은 복안대로 잘 진행되고 있어요.
examples.en: That work is going well, just as planned.

explain: '복안이 있다/없다'처럼 쓰는 일이 많고, 아직 밝히지 않은 속마음의 계획이라는 느낌이 있어요. 그냥 '계획'보다 격식 있어서 뉴스나 회의에서 자주 들려요. 친구끼리는 '생각이 있어' 정도로 말해요.
explain_en: It is mostly used as '복안이 있다/없다' and feels like a plan one keeps to oneself and hasn't revealed yet. It is more formal than '계획' and is heard in news and meetings. Among friends people would just say something like '생각이 있어'.

examples.en: During rush hour, the bus is packed.
The family lived crowded together in a small house.
I like the sound of my family bustling about in the kitchen.
The market alley was bustling with customers.
It's vacation, so the kids will be bustling around at home.
The cafe is so crowded that it's hard to study.

explain: 좁은 곳에 사람이 많이 모여 어수선하게 움직일 때 써요. '북적거리다'와 비슷하고, 일상에서는 '북적거리다'를 더 자주 써요. 불편하다는 뜻뿐 아니라 사람 사는 정겨운 느낌으로도 말해요.
explain_en: Use it when many people are packed into a small space and moving around in a busy way. It is similar to '북적거리다', which is more common in daily speech. It can sound uncomfortable, but also warm, like lively family life.

examples.en: The market was crowded and bustling with people.
The family lived together in a cramped little house.

examples.ko: 명절 전날 부엌에서 복작복작 음식을 만들었어요.
examples.en: The day before the holiday, we bustled about making food in the kitchen.
The kids are gathered in a crowd, playing.
There is a joy in living together crowded as a family.
It was a bustling mess inside the restaurant.

explain: 사람이 많이 모여 어수선하게 움직이는 모습을 나타내는 부사예요. 일상에서는 '북적북적'도 자주 써요. 뒤에 '붐비다, 모이다, 살다'처럼 사람이 있는 동작이 와요.
explain_en: This adverb shows many people gathered and moving around busily. In daily speech '북적북적' is also common. It is followed by verbs about people such as '붐비다', '모이다' and '살다'.

examples.en: The world these days is so complex that it's hard to understand.

examples.ko: 이 사건이 일어난 이유는 아주 복잡다단해요.
examples.en: The reasons this incident happened are very complicated.
Many tangled emotions came rushing in all at once.

examples.ko: 현대 사회의 문제는 복잡다단하기 때문에 한 가지 답이 없어요.
examples.en: Because problems in modern society are so intricate, there is no single answer.

examples.ko: 그 두 나라의 관계는 복잡다단하게 얽혀 있어요.
examples.en: The relationship between those two countries is intricately entangled.
I gave up applying because of the complicated procedure.

explain: '복잡하다'보다 격식 있는 말로, 일이나 사정이 여러 갈래로 얽혀 있다는 느낌이에요. 사람이 붐비는 곳에는 쓰지 않고 상황, 감정, 관계에 써요. 말보다 글이나 뉴스에서 더 자주 나와요.
explain_en: It is more formal than '복잡하다' and suggests matters or circumstances tangled in many directions. It is used for situations, feelings and relationships, not for crowded places. It appears more in writing and news than in speech.

examples.ko: 이 문제의 복잡성을 쉽게 설명하기는 어려워요.
examples.en: It's hard to explain the complexity of this problem simply.
The complexity of the system keeps growing.
Because of the complexity, it's hard to learn how to use it.
People feel the complexity of a task differently.
Compared with the complexity of the design, the result is simple.

examples.ko: 복잡성보다 중요한 건 사용하기 쉬운 거예요.
examples.en: What matters more than complexity is being easy to use.

explain: 복잡한 정도나 성질을 말할 때 써요. 일상에서는 '복잡함'이나 '복잡하다'를 쓰고, '복잡성'은 보고서, 수업, 기술 이야기에서 많이 나와요. 반대말은 '단순성'이에요.
explain_en: It refers to the degree or nature of being complicated. In daily speech people say '복잡함' or '복잡하다', while '복잡성' appears in reports, classes and technical talk. The opposite is '단순성'.

examples.en: This painting is not the original but a reproduction.
The museum is displaying only replicas.

examples.ko: 복제물을 팔 때는 표시를 해야 해요.
examples.en: When selling reproductions, you must label them.
Even though it's a replica, it was made as delicately as the real thing.
It isn't easy to tell a copy from the original.
This replica is smaller than the original.

explain: 그림, 유물, 문서처럼 원본을 똑같이 다시 만든 것이에요. 반대말은 '원본'이나 '진품'이에요. 일상에서는 '복사본'이라고 더 쉽게 말해요.
explain_en: It refers to something made as an exact copy of an original, such as a painting, relic or document. The opposites are '원본' and '진품'. In daily speech people more simply say '복사본'.

examples.en: I repeated back the coordinates received by radio and confirmed them.

examples.ko: 복창 덕분에 번호를 잘못 들은 것을 바로 알았어요.
examples.en: Thanks to repeating it back, I immediately realized I had heard the number wrong.

examples.ko: 중요한 숫자는 복창 확인을 꼭 해 주세요. — 네, 알겠어요.
examples.en: Please be sure to repeat important numbers back to confirm. — Yes, understood.

examples.ko: 학생들이 선생님 지시를 큰 소리로 복창했어요.
examples.en: The students repeated the teacher's instructions aloud.

examples.ko: 주문을 받으면 손님 앞에서 메뉴를 복창해요.
examples.en: When taking an order, I repeat the menu items back in front of the customer.

examples.ko: 잘 들렸는지 확인하려고 제가 한 번 복창할게요.
examples.en: I'll repeat it once to check that I heard correctly.

explain: 들은 말을 그대로 소리 내어 되풀이해서 맞게 들었는지 확인할 때 써요. 군대, 무전, 주문 확인처럼 정확해야 하는 상황에서 많이 나와요. 그냥 따라 말하는 '따라 하다'와 달리 확인이 목적이에요.
explain_en: Use it when you repeat what you heard out loud to check that it was right. It often appears where accuracy matters, such as in the military, radio communication and order confirmation. Unlike '따라 하다' (just imitating), the purpose is confirmation.

examples.en: Construction gets into full swing from next month.
As competition got going in earnest, prices went down.
We need to prepare before the rainy season fully sets in.
Discussion of the new business has finally gotten into full swing.

examples.ko: 선거 운동이 곧 본격화될 거라고 해요.
examples.en: They say the election campaign will soon get into full swing.
I'll contact you again when the negotiations get serious.

explain: 일이나 흐름이 시작 단계를 지나 제대로 진행될 때 써요. 주어는 공사, 경쟁, 논의처럼 일이나 현상이에요. 사람이 의도를 갖고 하면 '본격화하다'를 써요.
explain_en: Use it when something moves past the starting stage and really gets going. The subject is an event or phenomenon, such as construction, competition or discussion. When a person does it on purpose, use '본격화하다'.

examples.en: The company steps up its overseas expansion from this year.
The government decided to start the support program in earnest.

examples.ko: 그 가수는 다음 달에 활동을 본격화할 거예요.
examples.en: That singer will begin full-scale activities next month.
Our team has now gotten serious about preparations.
At the stage of going full-scale, we need more people.

examples.ko: 연구를 본격화해서 내년에 결과를 낼 계획이에요.
examples.en: We plan to move the research into full gear and produce results next year.

explain: 사람이나 단체가 어떤 일을 제대로, 힘을 들여 시작할 때 써요. '활동을 본격화하다'처럼 목적어를 받아요. 일이 저절로 그렇게 되면 '본격화되다'를 써요.
explain_en: Use it when a person or group starts doing something properly and with real effort. It takes an object, as in '활동을 본격화하다'. When things simply develop that way on their own, use '본격화되다'.

examples.en: The new business has finally gotten on track.

examples.ko: 공사가 본궤도에 오르려면 시간이 더 걸려요.
examples.en: It will take more time for construction to get properly on track.
The economy is slowly returning to its normal course.
The project has settled onto its track, so I feel relieved.
It will take time for the economy to get back on track.
I put the derailed schedule back on track.

explain: '본궤도에 오르다/들어서다'처럼 거의 정해진 모양으로 써요. 시작 단계를 지나 일이 안정적으로 잘 굴러간다는 뜻이에요. 비슷하게 '궤도에 오르다'라고도 말해요.
explain_en: It is used almost only in set forms like '본궤도에 오르다/들어서다'. It means a matter has passed the starting stage and is running steadily. People also say '궤도에 오르다' in a similar way.

en: a lesson (to show someone); what one is made of

examples.ko: 이번 시합에서 상대 팀에 본때를 보여 줄 거예요.
examples.en: In this match, we'll show the other team what we're made of.

examples.ko: 한 번 본때를 보여 주면 다시는 안 그럴 거예요.
examples.en: If we teach him a lesson once, he won't do it again.

examples.ko: 저 사람한테 본때를 좀 보여 주고 싶어요.
examples.en: I want to teach that guy a lesson.
He said he'd show them a thing or two and left.

examples.ko: 실력으로 본때를 보여 주는 게 제일 멋있어요.
examples.en: Showing them with your skill is the coolest way.

examples.ko: 이번에는 정말 본때를 제대로 보여 줬어요.
examples.en: This time you really showed them properly.

explain: 거의 '본때를 보여 주다'의 모양으로만 써요. 잘못한 사람을 따끔하게 혼내거나, 실력을 확실히 보여 준다는 말투예요. 조금 거친 말이라 윗사람에게는 조심해서 써요.

phrases.en: Let's show them what we're made of this time.
phrases.nuance_ko: 상대가 다시는 얕보지 못하게 따끔하게 혼내거나 실력을 확실히 보여 준다는 뜻이에요. 조금 거친 말투예요.
phrases.nuance_en: It means to teach someone a lesson or clearly prove your ability so they won't look down on you again. The tone is a bit rough.
phrases.en_equiv: teach someone a lesson; show them what you're made of

explain_en: It is used almost only in the form '본때를 보여 주다'. It suggests sharply punishing someone who did wrong, or clearly proving your ability. It is a bit rough, so be careful when speaking to superiors.

examples.en: Kimchi really tastes best when you eat it on its home turf.

examples.ko: 본바닥 사람들이 가는 식당으로 가 봐요.
examples.en: Let's go to a restaurant where the locals go.

examples.ko: 저 선생님은 영어 본바닥에서 오래 공부하셨어요.
examples.en: That teacher studied for a long time where English is natively spoken.

examples.ko: 피자의 본바닥인 이탈리아에 가 보고 싶어요.
examples.en: I want to go to Italy, the home ground of pizza.

examples.ko: 본바닥 사람들한테 길을 물어보는 게 제일 빨라요.
examples.en: Asking the locals for directions is the fastest.
It tastes different because it's made with true local skill.

explain: 어떤 것이 처음 생기고 발달한 바로 그곳을 가리켜요. 구어체이고 약간 속된 느낌이 있어요. '본고장'과 비슷하게 쓰지만 '본바닥'이 더 편한 말투예요.
explain_en: It points to the very place where something originated and developed. It is colloquial and a little slangy. It is used much like '본고장', but '본바닥' sounds more casual.

examples.ko: 화장을 지우니 얼굴 본바탕이 그대로 보여요.
examples.en: When I wash off my makeup, my natural face shows through.
A person's true nature shows when times are hard.

examples.ko: 그 친구는 본바탕이 착해서 미워할 수가 없어요.
examples.en: That friend is good-natured at heart, so I can't hate him.
I think you should look at the essence rather than the appearance.

examples.ko: 이 색은 제 얼굴 본바탕과 잘 어울려요.
examples.en: This color suits the natural look of my face well.
No matter how much you dress up, the underlying nature doesn't change.

explain: 꾸미거나 손대기 전의 원래 모습이나 타고난 성질이에요. '본성'은 성격에 쓰지만 '본바탕'은 얼굴, 재료, 사람됨에도 폭넓게 써요. '본바탕이 좋다/착하다'처럼 자주 말해요.
explain_en: It means the original look or inborn quality before anything is added or changed. '본성' is for personality, but '본바탕' also covers faces, materials and character. It is often used like '본바탕이 좋다/착하다'.

examples.en: My father is by nature a man of few words.

examples.ko: 본시 그 길은 시장으로 가는 길이었어요.
examples.en: Originally that road was the way to the market.
We were neighbors to begin with, so we got close quickly.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 본시 욕심이 없는 사람이에요.
examples.en: He is by nature a person without greed.

examples.ko: 그 아이는 본시 겁이 많지 않았어요.
examples.en: That child was not timid by nature.

examples.ko: 본시 이 건물은 학교로 지었다고 해요.
examples.en: They say this building was originally built as a school.

explain: '본래, 원래'와 같은 뜻이지만 글이나 옛날식 말투에서 쓰는 말이에요. 대화에서는 '원래'가 훨씬 자연스러워요. '처음부터, 타고나기를'이라는 느낌으로 문장 앞이나 서술어 앞에 와요.
explain_en: It means the same as '본래' and '원래', but it belongs to writing and old-fashioned speech. In conversation, '원래' sounds much more natural. It comes at the start of a sentence or before a predicate, with the feel of 'from the beginning' or 'by nature'.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 항상 자기 본위로만 생각해요.
examples.en: He always thinks only in terms of himself.
I want to create a service that puts the customer first.

examples.ko: 편의 본위로 정하면 불편한 사람이 생겨요.
examples.en: If you decide based only on convenience, someone will be inconvenienced.
This gathering is centered on socializing.

examples.ko: 자기 본위인 태도는 팀 일에 도움이 안 돼요.
examples.en: A self-centered attitude doesn't help in teamwork.

examples.ko: 자기 본위에서 벗어나 다른 사람 입장도 생각해 보세요.
examples.en: Step away from being self-centered and think about others' positions too.

explain: 혼자 쓰지 않고 '자기 본위, 편의 본위, 손님 본위'처럼 앞말을 붙여 '그것을 가장 중심에 둔다'는 뜻을 나타내요. '자기 본위'는 이기적이라는 비판의 느낌이 있어요. 비슷한 말로 '중심'이 있어요.
explain_en: It is not used alone but after another word, as in '자기 본위', '편의 본위' and '손님 본위', to mean putting that thing at the center. '자기 본위' carries a criticism of being selfish. A similar word is '중심'.

examples.en: Today's business just barely broke even.
With stocks, even breaking even is a relief.
I worked hard, but in the end I only broke even.

examples.ko: 이 게임은 해 봐야 본전치기일 거예요.
examples.en: Even if you try this game, you'll probably only break even.
It's a pity that it ended with just breaking even.
This month's event was close to breaking even as well.

explain: 이익도 손해도 없이 들인 돈만 겨우 건졌다는 뜻으로, 구어에서 자주 써요. '손해는 안 봤다'는 안도와 '남는 게 없다'는 아쉬움이 같이 있어요. '본전'은 처음에 들인 돈이에요.
explain_en: It is a colloquial word meaning you only just got back the money you put in, with no profit and no loss. It carries both relief at not losing and disappointment at gaining nothing. '본전' is the original money invested.
